claim: On-Off direction-selective ganglion cells (On-Off DSGCs) have a spatially displaced glutamatergic receptive field along their horizontal preferred-null motion axes.
source: Here, we report that On-Off DSGCs have a spatially displaced glutamatergic receptive field along their horizontal preferred-null motion axes.
evidence: This is the main finding stated in the abstract, supported by experimental data shown in Figures 1-4.

claim: The displaced receptive field contributes to DSGC null-direction spiking during interrupted motion trajectories.
source: This displaced receptive field contributes to DSGC null-direction spiking during interrupted motion trajectories.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figures 5-6 showing null-direction responses during occluded motion.

claim: Population responses during interrupted motion may help populations of On-Off DSGCs signal the spatial location of moving objects in complex, naturalistic visual environments.
source: Theoretical analyses indicate that population responses during interrupted motion may help populations of On-Off DSGCs signal the spatial location of moving objects in complex, naturalistic visual environments.
evidence: This claim is based on computational modeling results shown in Figure 7.

claim: The direction-selective circuit exploits separate sets of mechanisms under different stimulus conditions.
source: Our study highlights that the direction-selective circuit exploits separate sets of mechanisms under different stimulus conditions, and these mechanisms may help encode multiple visual features.
evidence: This is a summary conclusion based on the experimental findings showing different responses to full-field vs. interrupted motion.

claim: Different visual stimuli can engage different mechanisms to shape the neuronal RF even at the earliest stage of visual processing in the retina.
source: It has been increasingly appreciated that different visual stimuli can engage different mechanisms to shape the neuronal RF even at the earliest stage of visual processing in the retina.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to previous work (Chiao and Masland, 2003; Demb et al., 1999; Deny et al., 2017; Huang et al., 2019; Olveczky et al., 2003; Takeshita and Gollisch, 2014; Yao et al., 2018).

claim: A DSGC fires maximally to visual stimuli moving across its RF in its preferred direction and is inhibited from firing by stimuli moving in the opposite, null direction.
source: A DSGC fires maximally to visual stimuli moving across its RF in its preferred direction and is inhibited from firing by stimuli moving in the opposite, null direction (Barlow and Hill, 1963; Barlow and Levick, 1965; Oyster, 1968).
evidence: This is a well-established property of DSGCs supported by classic citations.

claim: The direction-selective spiking is largely attributed to the GABAergic input from the starburst amacrine cell (SAC).
source: The direction-selective spiking is largely attributed to the GABAergic input from the starburst amacrine cell (SAC).
evidence: This is a well-established mechanism in the field, supported by the context and citations.

claim: SAC dendrites are inherently direction-selective, as they are activated by centrifugal motion, or motion from soma to dendritic tip.
source: SAC dendrites are inherently direction-selective, as they are activated by centrifugal motion, or motion from soma to dendritic tip (Euler et al., 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Euler et al., 2002.

claim: Only SAC dendrites that extend along the null direction of the DSGC selectively make GABAergic synapses with the DSGC.
source: Additionally, only SAC dendrites that extend along the null direction of the DSGC selectively make GABAergic synapses with the DSGC (Briggman et al., 2011; Fried et al., 2002; Lee et al., 2010; Wei et al., 2011; Yonehara et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by multiple citations describing the asymmetric wiring pattern.

claim: The asymmetry of inhibition evoked by motion in the preferred and null directions is important for the DSGC's direction selectivity.
source: The asymmetry of inhibition evoked by motion in the preferred and null directions is important for the DSGC's direction selectivity (Pei et al., 2015; Taylor and Vaney, 2002).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Pei et al., 2015 and Taylor and Vaney, 2002.

claim: On-Off DSGCs prefer motion in one of the four cardinal directions.
source: The most well-studied DSGC type, the On-Off DSGC, prefers motion in one of the four cardinal directions (Oyster and Barlow, 1967; Sabbah et al., 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Oyster and Barlow, 1967 and Sabbah et al., 2017.

claim: On-Off DSGCs have bistratified dendritic arbors in the On and Off sublamina of the inner plexiform layer (IPL) to extract motion directions of bright and dark signals, respectively.
source: They have bistratified dendritic arbors in the On and Off sublamina of the inner plexiform layer (IPL) to extract motion directions of bright and dark signals, respectively (Figure 1A; Famiglietti, 1983; He and Masland, 1998; Kittila and Massey, 1997).
evidence: This claim is supported by Figure 1A and citations to Famiglietti, 1983; He and Masland, 1998; Kittila and Massey, 1997.

claim: Peripheral spots evoked maximal spiking (Max) in some regions and minimal responses in opposite regions (Opp) across the dendritic span.
source: The spot stimulus delivered to the pDSGC RF periphery uncovered an asymmetric RF organization where some spots evoked maximal spiking (Max) and other spots presented to the opposite regions (Opp) across the dendritic span evoked minimal responses (Figure 1B–C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A-B).
evidence: This claim is directly supported by experimental data shown in Figure 1B-C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: The Max-Opp axis largely corresponds to the preferred-null motion axis.
source: The Max-Opp axis largely corresponds to the preferred-null motion axis, which is shown by the polar plots in Figure 1 where the preferred side is aligned to the top.
evidence: This claim is supported by the polar plots in Figure 1.

claim: The majority of the maximum responses to the peripheral spots occurs within 67.5 degrees from the preferred direction of the DSGC and half occur within 22.5 degrees of the preferred direction.
source: The majority of the maximum responses to the peripheral spots occurs within 67.5 degrees from the preferred direction of the DSGC and half occur within 22.5 degrees of the preferred direction (Figure 1B–C, 'Control', Figure 1—figure supplement 1A).
evidence: This claim is supported by data shown in Figure 1B-C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A.

claim: The displacement of the pDSGC spiking RF persists after blocking SAC inputs with DHβE and gabazine.
source: Under this condition, we still observed a spatial asymmetry in pDSGC spiking activity evoked by the flashing spots (Figure 1C, Figure 1—figure supplement 1A-B, 'DHβE and Gabazine'), indicating a spatial displacement of glutamatergic excitation of the pDSGC in the absence of SAC influence.
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data in Figure 1C and Figure 1—figure supplement 1A-B showing persistence of asymmetry after pharmacological blockade.

claim: Spot-evoked EPSCs show a spatial bias toward the preferred side.
source: Consistent with the pattern of pDSGC spiking activity, spot-evoked EPSCs show a spatial bias toward the preferred side (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and F, 'Control').
evidence: This claim is supported by EPSC recordings shown in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C and F.

claim: Isolation of the glutamatergic component of the EPSC by the addition of DHβE and gabazine confirms the persistence of the spatial asymmetry.
source: Isolation of the glutamatergic component of the EPSC by the addition of DHβE and gabazine confirms the persistence of the spatial asymmetry, indicating that the glutamatergic excitation of the pDSGC is not isotropic but is spatially displaced relative to the soma (Figure 1D, Figure 1—figure supplement 1C-G, 'DHβE and Gabazine').
evidence: This claim is supported by EPSC data in Figure 1D and Figure 1—figure supplement 1C-G after pharmacological isolation of glutamatergic inputs.

claim: Gabazine and DHβE reduced the rise and decay time of the EPSC waveform compared to that in the control condition.
source: We noted that gabazine and DHβE reduced the rise and decay time of the EPSC waveform compared to that in the control condition (Figure 1—figure supplement 1E), presumably due to the removal of the cholinergic component of the EPSC.
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 1—figure supplement 1E showing changes in EPSC kinetics.

claim: Dendritic arbors of pDSGCs do not exhibit a salient or consistent bias relative to the cell's preferred motion direction.
source: Consistent with previous studies, dendritic arbors of pDSGCs do not exhibit a salient or consistent bias relative to the cell's preferred motion direction.
evidence: This claim is supported by morphological analysis in Figure 2 and is consistent with previous studies.

claim: The total dendritic length or the number of dendritic branching points does not significantly differ between the preferred and null sides of the pDSGC dendritic field.
source: The total dendritic length or the number of dendritic branching points does not significantly differ between the preferred and null sides of the pDSGC dendritic field (Figure 2C–D, Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-C).
evidence: This claim is supported by quantitative morphological analysis shown in Figure 2C-D and Figure 2—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: There is a non-random skew of the pDSGC dendritic length and number of branch points toward the regions corresponding to light spots evoking the strongest glutamatergic EPSCs.
source: Indeed, we found a non-random skew of the pDSGC dendritic length and number of branch points toward the regions corresponding to light spots evoking the strongest glutamatergic EPSCs (Figure 2E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 2E showing correlation between dendritic distribution and EPSC strength.

claim: The pDSGC's excitatory RF is partially shaped by its dendritic morphology, rather than being completely independent of the cell's dendritic distribution.
source: This indicates that the pDSGC's excitatory RF is partially shaped by its dendritic morphology, rather than being completely independent of the cell's dendritic distribution.
evidence: This is an inference based on the correlation between dendritic distribution and EPSC patterns shown in Figure 2E.

claim: There is no positive correlation between the extent of EPSC bias and the extent of dendritic bias along the axis of maximal glutamatergic displacement.
source: When we examined the relationship between EPSC bias and dendritic arbor distribution along the axis of maximal glutamatergic displacement, we did not find a positive correlation between the extent of EPSC bias and the extent of dendritic bias (Figure 2F), suggesting that mechanisms other than dendritic arbor density also contribute to the displacement of the pDSGC glutamatergic RF.
evidence: This claim is supported by the lack of correlation shown in Figure 2F.

claim: The center of the glutamatergic EPSC RF is displaced from the center of the dendritic field for most cells.
source: Notably, for most cells, the center of the glutamatergic EPSC RF is displaced from the center of the dendritic field (Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-B), indicating additional mechanisms underlying the glutamatergic RF displacement apart from the dendritic arbor distribution.
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 3—figure supplement 1A-B showing spatial mismatch between RF center and dendritic center.

claim: The EPSC density on the displaced side of the dendritic field is larger than the corresponding region on the opposite side.
source: When we calculated the density along the axis of maximal glutamatergic RF displacement, we found that the EPSC density on the displaced side of the dendritic field is larger than the corresponding region on the opposite side (Figure 3E, left, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by EPSC density analysis shown in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E.

claim: From 50 μm away from the soma, spots on the side corresponding to the maximum displacement yield stronger EPSCs than spots on the opposite side, while controlling for the same dendritic length.
source: From 50 μm away from the soma, spots on the side corresponding to the maximum displacement (Maximum) yield stronger EPSCs than spots on the opposite side (Opposite), while controlling for the same dendritic length (Figure 3E, right, Figure 3—figure supplement 1E).
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 3E and Figure 3—figure supplement 1E showing differential EPSC strength normalized by dendritic length.

claim: There is no marked gradient in ribbon density across the preferred-null motion axis of the three reconstructed On-Off DSGCs.
source: We found no marked gradient in ribbon density across the preferred-null motion axis of the three cells (Figure 4D–F, Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-B), suggesting that the gradient in EPSC density across this axis is not determined by the density of bipolar inputs.
evidence: This claim is supported by electron microscopy reconstruction data shown in Figure 4D-F and Figure 4—figure supplement 1A-B.

claim: There are no significant differences in the latency, rise and decay times in EPSC waveforms across the axis of maximal glutamatergic RF displacement.
source: We found no significant differences in the latency, rise and decay times in EPSC waveforms across the axis of maximal glutamatergic RF displacement in response to the small flashing spots (Figure 4G–I, left panels).
evidence: This claim is supported by kinetic analysis shown in Figure 4G-I.

claim: There is no monotonic change in glutamatergic EPSC kinetics along the preferred-null motion axis in DHβE and gabazine or in DHβE only.
source: In addition, we did not detect a monotonic change in glutamatergic EPSC kinetics along the preferred-null motion axis in DHβE and gabazine (Figure 4G–I, right panels) or in DHβE only (Figure 4—figure supplement 1C-D).
evidence: This claim is supported by kinetic analysis shown in Figure 4G-I and Figure 4—figure supplement 1C-D.

claim: The kinetics of bipolar cell signals onto On-Off pDSGCs do not differ substantially along the preferred-null motion axis.
source: Thus, our data suggest that the kinetics of bipolar cell signals onto On-Off pDSGCs do not differ substantially along the preferred-null motion axis.
evidence: This is an inference based on the lack of kinetic differences shown in Figure 4.

claim: Cells with more spatially separated excitatory and inhibitory receptive fields were more direction-selective.
source: By comparing the onset times of EPSCs and IPSCs to preferred-direction motion, we found that cells with more spatially separated excitatory and inhibitory receptive fields were more direction-selective (Figure 7—figure supplement 1L).
evidence: This claim is supported by correlation analysis shown in Figure 7—figure supplement 1L.

claim: The occluded motion stimulus caused both preferred and null-direction spiking responses.
source: In contrast to the full-field motion stimulus, the occluded motion stimulus caused both preferred and null-direction spiking responses (Figure 5B, Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-C).
evidence: This claim is supported by experimental data shown in Figure 5B and Figure 5—figure supplement 1A-C.

claim: Responses to the occluded motion stimulus are only evoked when the bar travels in the preferred side, which corresponds to the displaced side of the pDSGC RF.
source: These responses are only evoked when the bar travels in the preferred side, which corresponds to the displaced side of the pDSGC RF (Figure 5B, middle row, and 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 5B and 5C showing regional specificity of responses.

claim: No spiking response is evoked when the bar moves across to the null side beyond the occluder.
source: In contrast, no spiking response is evoked when the bar moves across to the null side beyond the occluder (Figure 5B, bottom row, Figure 5C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 5B and 5C showing lack of response on the null side.

claim: The regional difference in responses to occluded motion persists after blocking cholinergic and GABAergic transmission with DHβE and gabazine.
source: To test whether this regional difference is due to the asymmetric wiring between SACs and DSGCs, we blocked the cholinergic and GABAergic transmission with DHβE and gabazine and saw that the regional difference persisted (Figure 5C, Figure 5—figure supplement 1B).
evidence: This claim is supported by pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 5C and Figure 5—figure supplement 1B.

claim: IPSC responses to the occluded bar stimulus are displaced to the opposite side compared to EPSC responses.
source: In contrast, IPSC responses to the occluded bar stimulus are displaced to the opposite side compared to EPSC responses (Figure 5—figure supplement 1D), consistent with the asymmetric wiring pattern from SACs from the null side to the DSGC (Briggman et al., 2011; Fried et al., 2002; Lee et al., 2010; Wei et al., 2011; Yonehara et al., 2011).
evidence: This claim is supported by IPSC data in Figure 5—figure supplement 1D and citations describing asymmetric wiring.

claim: The spatial asymmetry of the spike response remains during the occluded motion stimulus after individually blocking GABAC receptor activity, glycine receptor activity, and gap-junction coupling.
source: Moreover, we individually blocked each of several types of signaling, including GABAC receptor activity, glycine receptor activity, and gap-junction coupling with TPMPA, strychnine, MFA, and Carbenoxolone, respectively, and found that the spatial asymmetry of the spike response remains during the occluded motion stimulus (Figure 5—figure supplement 1H-K).
evidence: This claim is supported by pharmacological experiments shown in Figure 5—figure supplement 1H-K.

claim: The asymmetric glutamatergic RF of the pDSGC contributes to robust spiking in both null and preferred directions when the preferred side of the RF is activated by the occluded motion stimulus.
source: Based on these pharmacology results, we conclude that the asymmetric glutamatergic RF of the pDSGC contributes to robust spiking in both null and preferred directions when the preferred side of the RF is activated by the occluded motion stimulus.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the pharmacological experiments in Figure 5.

claim: aDSGCs exhibit a null-direction response to the occluded motion stimulus that is similar to that of pDSGCs.
source: Notably, aDSGCs also exhibited a null-direction response to the occluded motion stimulus that is similar to that of pDSGCs (Figure 5H, Figure 5—figure supplement 2D), indicating that aDSGC RFs are also displaced to the preferred side.
evidence: This claim is supported by calcium imaging data in Figure 5H and Figure 5—figure supplement 2D.

claim: There is an increase in both the spike number and the firing rate as the starting position of the moving bar is located past the soma on the preferred side of the pDSGC RF for null-direction moving bars.
source: For the null-direction moving bar, there is an increase in both the spike number and the firing rate as the starting position of the moving bar is located past the soma on the preferred side of the pDSGC RF (Figure 6A–C).
evidence: This claim is supported by data in Figure 6A-C showing position-dependent responses.

claim: The null-direction response of the pDSGC during the occluded motion stimulus is dependent on the position in the receptive field from which the moving edge emerges, not the previous motion approaching the occluder.
source: These results illustrate that the null-direction response of the pDSGC during the occluded motion stimulus is dependent on the position in the receptive field from which the moving edge emerges, not the previous motion approaching the occluder.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the emergent bar experiments shown in Figure 6.

claim: When a moving object appears and starts moving on the preferred side of the pDSGC's RF, this DSGC would generate a null-direction spiking response together with the preferred-direction response of a nearby On-Off DSGC subtype preferring the opposite motion direction.
source: In particular, if a moving object emerging from behind an occluder activates the preferred side of an On-Off DSGC's RF, this DSGC would generate a null-direction spiking response together with the preferred-direction response of a nearby On-Off DSGC subtype preferring the opposite motion direction (Figure 7A).
evidence: This is a hypothesis illustrated in Figure 7A and tested through computational modeling.

claim: Synchronous spiking activity between DSGCs of opposite preferred directions could yield a stronger and more localized spatial signal at the population level at the location of motion interruption.
source: Such synchronous spiking activity between DSGCs of opposite preferred directions could yield a stronger and more localized spatial signal at the population level at the location of motion interruption.
evidence: This is a hypothesis tested through computational modeling in Figure 7.

claim: When the moving bar emerges from behind the occluder, null-direction responses from the pDSGCs undergoing partial RF activation on the preferred side transiently degrades the population estimate of the motion direction.
source: Our modeling results show that when the moving bar emerges from behind the occluder, null-direction responses from the pDSGCs undergoing partial RF activation on the preferred side transiently degrades the population estimate of the motion direction as would be expected (Figure 7C and E).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 7C and E.

claim: The coincidence of the null-direction responses from pDSGCs and the preferred-direction response of neighboring aDSGCs when the bar exits the occlusion substantially improves the estimation of bar position.
source: However, the coincidence of the null-direction responses from pDSGCs and the preferred-direction response of neighboring aDSGCs when the bar exits the occlusion substantially improves the estimation of bar position at this time (Figure 7B and D).
evidence: This claim is supported by computational modeling results shown in Figure 7B and D.

claim: For a bar traveling at the speed of 330 μm/s, the synchronous firing between pDSGCs and the neighboring aDSGCs reduces the error in the population estimate of the bar edge's spatial position by over 80 percent.
source: For a bar traveling at the speed of 330 μm/s (the lowest speed in our experiments and simulations), the synchronous firing between pDSGCs and the neighboring aDSGCs reduces the error in the population estimate of the bar edge's spatial position by over 80 percent.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the computational modeling.

claim: At the highest speed of 2640 μm/s, there was still around a 40% decrease in position estimation error during the occlusion trials.
source: At the highest speed of 2640 μm/s, there was still around a 40% decrease in position estimation error during the occlusion trials.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the computational modeling.

claim: The absolute position error decrease was around 3 degrees of visual angle, or around half the receptive field size of an On-Off DSGC, across bar speeds in models with low levels of background noise.
source: The absolute position error decrease was around 3 degrees of visual angle, or around half the receptive field size of an On-Off DSGC, across bar speeds in models with low levels of background noise.
evidence: This is a quantitative result from the computational modeling.

claim: At the site of motion interruption, the DSGC population response transiently prioritizes the encoding of the emerging moving object position over its motion direction.
source: Therefore, at the site of motion interruption, the DSGC population response transiently prioritizes the encoding of the emerging moving object position over its motion direction.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the computational modeling results in Figure 7.

claim: The accuracy of estimating position from contrast changes is the same for populations with asymmetric receptive fields and populations with symmetric receptive fields.
source: We found that the accuracy of estimating position from contrast changes is the same for populations with asymmetric receptive fields and populations with symmetric receptive fields.
evidence: This is a result from computational analysis comparing different RF configurations.

claim: The detection of the contrast change would only improve if the receptive field size decreased.
source: The detection of the contrast change would only improve if the receptive field size decreased (data not shown).
evidence: This is a result from computational analysis.

claim: Directed motion is required for an improvement in position estimation because a null-direction signal can only occur in a small region on the preferred side.
source: Directed motion is required for an improvement in position estimation because a null-direction signal can only occur in a small region on the preferred side.
evidence: This is an inference based on the computational modeling results.

claim: The synchrony of the null-direction and preferred-direction signals within the population yields a more spatially constrained signal necessary for fine spatial discrimination of moving stimuli.
source: Therefore, the synchrony of the null-direction and preferred-direction signals within the population yields a more spatially constrained signal necessary for fine spatial discrimination of moving stimuli.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the computational modeling results.

claim: The decoder correctly identified occlusion trials with more than 99% accuracy in conditions with background firing rates of 10 spikes/s or less.
source: In conditions with background firing rates of 10 spikes/s or less, the decoder correctly identified occlusion trials with more than 99% accuracy (Figure 7H).
evidence: This claim is supported by the coincidence detection model results shown in Figure 7H.

claim: The synchrony of preferred-direction responses from one DSGC subtype and the null-direction responses from the opposite DSGC subtype during interrupted motion conditions can be easily detected.
source: This coincidence detection model suggests that the synchrony of preferred-direction responses from one DSGC subtype and the null-direction responses from the opposite DSGC subtype during interrupted motion conditions can be easily detected.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the coincidence detection model results in Figure 7H.

claim: The salient synchrony signal can potentially inform downstream visual areas of the type of motion that is occurring or provide an alarm signal to the animal that there is an unexpected change in their environment.
source: This salient synchrony signal can potentially inform downstream visual areas of the type of motion that is occurring or provide an alarm signal to the animal that there is an unexpected change in their environment.
evidence: This is a speculative interpretation of the modeling results.

claim: A spatial displacement of glutamatergic inputs to the preferred side of the On-Off pDSGCs is due to a non-uniform distribution of synaptic conductances across the pDSGC dendritic span.
source: Our study reveals a new form of asymmetry in the direction-selective circuit: a spatial displacement of glutamatergic inputs to the preferred side of the On-Off pDSGCs due to a non-uniform distribution of synaptic conductances across the pDSGC dendritic span.
evidence: This is a summary of the main finding supported by data in Figures 1-4.

claim: Occluded motion stimuli reduce the contribution of SAC-mediated inputs to allow the excitatory receptive field to dominate the spiking response in a non-directional manner when only part of the RF is stimulated.
source: In contrast to full-field continuous motion which maximizes the contribution of SAC-mediated null-direction inhibition, occluded motion stimuli reduce the contribution of SAC-mediated inputs to allow the excitatory receptive field to dominate the spiking response in a non-directional manner when only part of the RF is stimulated.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental results in Figures 5-6.

claim: An On-Off DSGC's response to occluded motion stimuli is determined both by how much of the receptive field is activated and where that activation occurs.
source: Therefore, an On-Off DSGC's response to occluded motion stimuli is determined both by how much of the receptive field is activated and where that activation occurs.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the experimental results in Figures 5-6.

claim: The gradient of glutamatergic current density across the pDSGC dendritic span may arise from varying strengths of individual glutamatergic synapses, heterogeneous membrane properties across pDSGC dendritic field, and contribution from Vglut3+ amacrine cells.
source: The gradient of glutamatergic current density across the pDSGC dendritic span may arise from a number of possible scenarios including varying strengths of individual glutamatergic synapses, heterogeneous membrane properties across pDSGC dendritic field, and contribution from Vglut3 +amacrine cells (Franke et al., 2017; Kim et al., 2015; Lee et al., 2016; ).
evidence: This is speculation about possible mechanisms, supported by citations to relevant literature.

claim: When motion trajectories are not continuous, the null-direction responses from cells near the occlusion edge transiently improves the encoding of location at the expense of direction encoding.
source: When motion trajectories are not continuous, the null-direction responses from cells near the occlusion edge transiently improves the encoding of location at the expense of direction encoding.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the computational modeling results in Figure 7.

claim: The trade-off between positional and directional encoding, which occurs when an object emerges from behind another object, may reflect the animal's greater need for positional information of the emerging object than the direction in which it is moving.
source: We speculate that the trade-off between positional and directional encoding, which occurs when an object emerges from behind another object, may reflect the animal's greater need for positional information of the emerging object than the direction in which it is moving.
evidence: This is speculation about the functional significance of the findings.

claim: The synchronous response of null-direction and preferred-direction spiking can potentially provide a salient alarm signal for discontinuous motion, which may help the animal quickly attend to the site of the change.
source: Additionally, the synchronous response of null-direction and preferred-direction spiking can potentially provide a salient alarm signal for discontinuous motion, which may help the animal quickly attend to the site of the change.
evidence: This is speculation about the functional significance supported by the coincidence detection model.

claim: The population activity across cell types can help resolve ambiguities in single-cell responses.
source: Our findings that the population activity across cell types can help resolve ambiguities in single-cell responses share a common theme with previous modeling experiments from Kühn and Gollisch, 2019, which show that multiple DSGC subtypes with different motion direction tuning in the salamander retina are needed to isolate motion-related information from confounding contrast signals under complex texture motion.
evidence: This is a comparison with previous work (Kühn and Gollisch, 2019) to contextualize the findings.

claim: Specific stimulus patterns, such as occluded motion and 'reverse-phi' illusory motion with alternating contrast polarities, trigger null-direction responses in direction-selective neurons to serve context-specific encoding tasks that may be beneficial for extracting visual information from more complex natural scenes.
source: For example, specific stimulus patterns, such as occluded motion in our study and the 'reverse-phi' illusory motion with alternating contrast polarities studied in flies, trigger null-direction responses in direction-selective neurons to serve context-specific encoding tasks that may be beneficial for extracting visual information from more complex natural scenes (Salazar-Gatzimas et al., 2018; Agrochao et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a comparison with work in flies (Salazar-Gatzimas et al., 2018; Agrochao et al., 2020) to contextualize the findings.

claim: Local motion detection can be carried out by neuronal populations with wider receptive fields.
source: As another example, both previous studies in flies and our study indicate that local motion detection can be carried out by neuronal populations with wider receptive fields (Fisher et al., 2015).
evidence: This is a comparison with work in flies (Fisher et al., 2015) to contextualize the findings.

claim: Partial RF activation on the preferred side of the pDSGC generates a non-directional, local contrast response that may contribute to a salient population signal from the retina to the brain to alert the animal about emerging motion.
source: In our model, partial RF activation on the preferred side of the pDSGC generates a non-directional, local contrast response that may contribute to a salient population signal from the retina to the brain to alert the animal about emerging motion.
evidence: This is an interpretation of the modeling results in the context of function.

claim: Local contrast response properties of direction-selective neurons in the fly visual system have been shown to profoundly modulate their motion computations and contribute to visually guided behavior.
source: Interestingly, local contrast response properties of direction-selective neurons in the fly visual system have been shown to profoundly modulate their motion computations and contribute to visually guided behavior (Clark et al., 2014; Drews et al., 2020; Matulis et al., 2020).
evidence: This is a citation to work in flies (Clark et al., 2014; Drews et al., 2020; Matulis et al., 2020) to provide context.

claim: On-Off DSGCs are considered encoders of local motion, and project to the superficial layer of the superior colliculus (SC) and the shell region of the dorsal lateral geniculate nucleus (dLGN).
source: In contrast to the mammalian On DSGC that encodes global motion during optic flow and participates in the optokinetic reflex, On-Off DSGCs are considered encoders of local motion, and project to the superficial layer of the superior colliculus (SC) and the shell region of the dorsal lateral geniculate nucleus (dLGN) (Cruz-Martín et al., 2014; Huberman et al., 2009; Kay et al., 2011; Rivlin-Etzion et al., 2011).
evidence: This is a statement about known projection patterns supported by citations (Cruz-Martín et al., 2014; Huberman et al., 2009; Kay et al., 2011; Rivlin-Etzion et al., 2011).

claim: In the SC, On-Off DSGC inputs give rise to the direction selectivity of postsynaptic collicular neurons.
source: In the SC, On-Off DSGC inputs give rise to the direction selectivity of postsynaptic collicular neurons (Shi et al., 2017), indicating that these collicular neurons do not receive retinal inputs from a broad range of RGC types, but specifically from On-Off DSGCs.
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Shi et al., 2017.

claim: The superficial layer of the SC is well recognized for its roles in encoding spatial locations and instructing stimulus-directed defensive and prey behaviors.
source: Since the superficial layer of the SC is well recognized for its roles in encoding spatial locations and instructing stimulus-directed defensive and prey behaviors (Basso et al., 2021; Ito and Feldheim, 2018), the encoding of the spatial location of an emerging moving object by On-Off DSGCs may benefit rapid sensorimotor decisions that involve collicular circuitry.
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Basso et al., 2021 and Ito and Feldheim, 2018.

claim: The encoding of the spatial location of an emerging moving object by On-Off DSGCs may benefit rapid sensorimotor decisions that involve collicular circuitry.
source: Since the superficial layer of the SC is well recognized for its roles in encoding spatial locations and instructing stimulus-directed defensive and prey behaviors (Basso et al., 2021; Ito and Feldheim, 2018), the encoding of the spatial location of an emerging moving object by On-Off DSGCs may benefit rapid sensorimotor decisions that involve collicular circuitry.
evidence: This is speculation about functional significance based on known SC function.

claim: Other ganglion cell types such as W3 RGCs and HD-RGCs may also participate in fine spatial discrimination.
source: It is likely that other ganglion cell types also participate in fine spatial discrimination. For example, certain types of small receptive field RGCs such as W3 RGCs and HD-RGCs may also be well-suited to encode object location (Jacoby and Schwartz, 2017; Kim et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2012).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to Jacoby and Schwartz, 2017; Kim et al., 2010; Zhang et al., 2012.

claim: W3 RGCs are activated only in specific instances where the background is completely uniform, whereas On-Off DSGCs can be activated in a wide range of visual environments, including environments with noisy backgrounds.
source: It is worth noting that W3 RGCs are activated only in specific instances where the background is completely uniform, whereas On-Off DSGCs can be activated in a wide range of visual environments, including environments with noisy backgrounds (Chen et al., 2016; Chen et al., 2020).
evidence: This claim is supported by citations to Chen et al., 2016 and Chen et al., 2020.

claim: Computational modeling experiments have shown that the errors in object location between On-Off DSGCs after motion interruption and HD-RGCs are very similar in scale.
source: HD-RGCs also have small receptive fields, and computational modeling experiments have shown that the errors in object location between On-Off DSGCs after motion interruption and HD-RGCs are very similar in scale (Jacoby and Schwartz, 2017).
evidence: This claim is supported by citation to Jacoby and Schwartz, 2017.

claim: The position information encoded by other position encoders such as W3 and HD-RGCs may not be available to the specific downstream circuits that receive On-Off DSGC inputs.
source: However, given the divergent and type-specific central projection patterns of mouse ganglion cell types (Dhande et al., 2015; Ellis et al., 2016; Martersteck et al., 2017), the position information encoded by other position encoders such as W3 and HD-RGCs may not be available to the specific downstream circuits that receive On-Off DSGC inputs.
evidence: This is speculation based on known projection patterns cited from Dhande et al., 2015; Ellis et al., 2016; Martersteck et al., 2017.

claim: The population response of On-Off DSGCs after a motion interruption helps On-Off RGCs achieve the same performance as other ganglion cell populations implicated in fine spatial discrimination.
source: Our modeling study suggests that the population response of On-Off DSGCs after a motion interruption helps On-Off RGCs achieve the same performance as other ganglion cell populations implicated in fine spatial discrimination.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the computational modeling results.

claim: On-Off DSGCs may participate in different visual processing tasks compared to other ganglion cell types by projecting to different areas for implementing different responses.
source: On-Off DSGCs may participate in different visual processing tasks compared to other ganglion cell types by projecting to different areas for implementing different responses (Kay et al., 2011; Sanes and Masland, 2015).
evidence: This is speculation supported by citations to Kay et al., 2011 and Sanes and Masland, 2015.

claim: On-Off DSGCs could provide complementary information about the spatial location of moving objects when considered with other RGC populations.
source: Or, they could provide complementary information about the spatial location of moving objects when considered with other RGC populations.
evidence: This is speculation about possible functional roles.

claim: The information of spatial location is contained within the On-Off DSGC population response.
source: In either scenario, our theoretical analysis indicates that the information of spatial location is contained within the On-Off DSGC population response, and that it is possible that higher visual centers stand to benefit from this information.
evidence: This is a conclusion based on the computational modeling results.

claim: Elucidating the roles of diverse RGC types in motion encoding requires a thorough understanding of visual signal transformations along the processing pathways and how the visual system instructs visually guided behavior.
source: Ultimately, elucidating the roles of diverse RGC types in motion encoding requires a thorough understanding of visual signal transformations along the processing pathways and how the visual system instructs visually guided behavior.
evidence: This is a general statement about future research directions.
